entries.title: The second bulk-boundary factor must use the surviving boundary point
entries.locator: arXiv:1011.5822v3, Proposition4.1, equation(20), printed p.11/PDF index10; HTML section4. Versioned HTML and extracted PDF compared17 November2026; no visual-PDF or journal comparison. entries.claim: The factorization of P4(u1,u3,w)^2 uses P3(u1,w)P3(u2,w)P2(u1,u3).
entries.problem: The definitions have already sent u2 to u1; the surviving boundary pair is u1,u3. The second factor must depend on u3. The density formulas(21)–(23) give that dependence explicitly. For u1=0,u3=2,w=i, replacing the correct P3(2,i) by P3(0,i) multiplies the right-hand side by 5^(1/3).
entries.correction: Replace P3(u2,w) by P3(u3,w) in(20). XCYH derives the corrected identity directly from the stated densities using sin(zeta)=(u3-u1)Im(w)/(|w-u1||w-u3|), and evaluates the unchanged K_F. This is an index repair, not a change to the intended theorem or its constant.
entries.leanImpact: Distinguish the shrinking-interval endpoint from the two retained boundary points. The algebraic identity is available with explicit density hypotheses; their SLE derivation and the continuum-to-discrete passage remain separate inputs. No compiled association, author confirmation or journal-text correction is claimed.

resolution.summary: Use the surviving boundary mark u3 in the density factor.
resolution.impact: An index correction; the factorization constant is unchanged.

entries.title: The conditional bulk function has no boundary conformal factor
entries.locator: arXiv:1011.5822v3, Introduction, display after Theorem 1.1 and definitions (1)–(4), printed p.2/PDF index1. Versioned HTML and extracted PDF text compared 17 November 2026; no visual-PDF or journal comparison. Subsequent comparison, 20 November 2026: published Communications in Mathematical Physics 310 (2012), display following Theorem 1.1, p.612, with (1)–(4). Matching discrepancy in extracted journal PDF text; no visual-PDF check.
entries.claim: The conditional function F transforms with both the boundary factor |phi prime(v)|^(1/3) and the bulk factor |phi prime(w)|^(5/48).
entries.problem: F is normalized by the boundary-event probability. Its boundary density factor cancels in this quotient. Formula (4) has dilation degree -5/48; applying the printed covariance to phi(z)=c z in H would give F=c^(1/3)F for positive F.
entries.correction: Use only the bulk derivative factor for F. The joint density C F transforms with both factors. QLZ6 proves the quotient rule while retaining the order of the density limits.
entries.leanImpact: Keep conditional and joint density types and normalizations separate in any future interface. No compiled correspondence or author confirmation is claimed; the intended factorization formula is not disproved.

resolution.summary: Cancel the boundary covariance factor in the conditional quotient.
resolution.impact: Corrects the conditional transformation law; the joint factorization survives.

entries.title: The differential of the normalized density needs its current density factor
entries.locator: arXiv:1011.5822v3, section 3, unnumbered display for dD_t immediately after Girsanov, printed p.6/PDF index5. Versioned HTML and extracted PDF text compared 17 November 2026. Subsequent comparison, 20 November 2026: published Communications in Mathematical Physics 310 (2012), Section 3, unnumbered dD_t display following Girsanov, p.616. Matching discrepancy in extracted journal PDF text; no visual-PDF check.
entries.claim: With D_t=q_t/q_0, the source writes dD_t=sqrt(6) (partial_u q_t/q_t) dB_t.
entries.problem: The displayed coefficient is the stochastic logarithm coefficient. Differentiating the normalized conditional probability gives sqrt(6) partial_u q_t/q_0 instead, which is D_t times the printed expression.
entries.correction: Write dD_t=D_t sqrt(6) partial_u log(q_t) dB_t. Dividing its covariation by D_t in Girsanov then gives the intended drift already printed in the next display. W3QF proves this with compact stopping and the limiting boundary-density weight.
entries.leanImpact: Distinguish a density martingale from its stochastic logarithm. Verify the initial normalization, stopped true-martingale property and covariation before changing measure. No global terminal conditioning, compiled association or author confirmation is inferred.

resolution.summary: Include the current density in its stochastic differential.
resolution.impact: A local martingale calculation changes; the subsequent Girsanov drift is already correct.

entries.title: The boundary potential in the joint differential operator is inverse-square
entries.locator: arXiv:1011.5822v3, Theorem 3.2, equation (13) and following proof, printed pp.7–8/PDF indices6–7; compare equation (5), printed p.3. Versioned HTML and extracted PDF text compared 17 November 2026. Subsequent comparison, 20 November 2026: published Communications in Mathematical Physics 310 (2012), Theorem 3.2, (13) and its proof, pp.617–618; compare (5), p.613. Matching discrepancy in extracted journal PDF text; no visual-PDF check.
entries.claim: The operator annihilating C F contains the potential -2/(3(v-u)) with a first-power denominator.
entries.problem: The boundary density equation (5) has the inverse-square potential. The product rule leaves precisely that term when the conditioning drift cancels. The printed operator differs by (2/3)((v-u)^(-2)-(v-u)^(-1)); at gap 2 it sends a positive solution of the intended equation to -C F/6.
entries.correction: Replace every occurrence of this potential in (13) and its proof by -2/(3(v-u)^2). ES94 proves the resulting product identity exactly from the boundary density equation.
entries.leanImpact: Preserve the inverse-square factor in any generator or martingale interface; it has the same scaling degree as the second-order term. This repairs a differential-operator display, without claiming a completed SLE terminal proof or a compiled association.

resolution.summary: Use the inverse-square boundary potential in the joint equation.
resolution.impact: Corrects the displayed operator to the one furnished by the product rule.
